title.en: The Dwarf of Uxmal and the House of the Diviner
title.zh: 烏斯馬爾的侏儒與占卜者之屋

region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾

texts.period: Collected from local tradition c. 1840 (Stephens 1841-43); retold by Charnay 1887

source.work: Desire Charnay, The Ancient Cities of the New World (1887), reproducing the legend collected by John Lloyd Stephens (Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, 1843)

summary.en: A childless old woman hatches a dwarf from an egg; he grows wise but not tall. In trials of strength before the king he matches every feat — the stone, the bundles of cogoiol wood beaten on the head — because his mother's tortilla protects him. Ordered to build a palace taller than any other overnight, he wakes in the finished palace that still stands at Uxmal; the second blow of his little hand breaks the king's skull, and the people proclaim the dwarf their sovereign.
summary.zh: 無子的老嫗自一枚蛋孵出侏儒；他聰慧過人卻不再長高。國王面前，他力試屢勝——舉石、以硬木束互擊頭顱——因其母的玉米餅護其頭。國王限其一夜建成高於一切的宮殿，翌晨侏儒已睡於竣工的宮殿之中——即烏斯馬爾今存的占卜者之屋；而他小手的第二擊便碎了國王的頭顱，眾人遂擁侏儒為王。

sensitivity.note: Yucatec folk legend recorded by travelers; paraphrase of public-domain texts only.

passages.text: An old woman lived alone in her hut, rarely leaving her chimney-corner. She was much distressed at having no children; in her grief, one day she took an egg, wrapped it up carefully in a cotton cloth, and put it in a corner of her hut. She looked at it every day with great anxiety; one morning, however, she found the shell broken, and a lovely tiny creature was stretching out its arms to her.
passages.note: Quoted from Charnay (1887) reproducing Stephens (1843); lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: The old woman was in raptures; she took it to her heart, gave it a nurse, and was so careful of it that at the end of a year the baby walked and talked as well as a grown-up man, but he stopped growing. She exclaimed that the baby should be a great chief, and one day told him to go to the king's palace and engage him in a trial of strength. The dwarf begged hard not to be sent on such an enterprise, but the old woman insisted, and he was obliged to obey.
passages.note: Condensed from Charnay (1887) reproducing Stephens (1843); not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: The king smiled and asked him to lift a stone of three arobes; the child returned crying to his mother, who sent him back, saying: 'If the king can lift the stone, you can lift it too.' The king did take it up, but so did the dwarf. His strength was tried in many other ways, but all the king did was as easily done by the dwarf. Wroth at being outdone by so puny a creature, the prince told the dwarf that unless he built a palace loftier than any in the city, he should die.
passages.note: Condensed from Charnay (1887) reproducing Stephens (1843); not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: The affrighted dwarf returned to the old woman, who bade him not despair, and the next morning they both awoke in the palace which is still standing. The king, amazed, sent for the dwarf to collect two bundles of cogoiol, with one of which he would strike the dwarf on the head and consent to be struck in return. The old woman placed a tortilla on his head. The king broke his whole bundle on the dwarf's head without hurting him in the least; the dwarf struck, and at the second blow the king's skull was broken to pieces. The spectators immediately proclaimed the victorious dwarf their sovereign.
passages.note: Condensed from Charnay (1887) reproducing Stephens (1843); not verbatim throughout.

texts.canonical_translation: Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan (1843), via Charnay (1887)

narrative.en:
The dwarf legend is the signature folk narrative of Uxmal, told to John Lloyd Stephens at the ruins in 1841-43 and retold by Desiré Charnay from his pages. A childless old woman, alone in her hut, grieves that she has no children; one day she takes an egg, wraps it in a cotton cloth, and sets it in a corner of her hut. It does not change until one morning the shell is broken and a tiny, lovely creature stretches out its arms to her. She gives it a nurse and tends it so carefully that within a year the baby walks and talks like a grown man — but then he stops growing. In her joy the old woman declares the child will be a great chief, and sends him to the king's palace to engage the sovereign in a trial of strength.

The trials follow the folk-tale pattern of the outwitted king. The king bids the dwarf lift a stone of three arobes; the child runs home crying, but his mother sends him back with the words 'If the king can lift it, you can lift it too' — and the dwarf lifts what the king lifts, and matches every feat. Furious at being outdone by a puny creature, the king sets a deadly condition: build a palace loftier than any in the city overnight, or die. The old woman forbids despair, and the next morning the dwarf awakes in the completed palace — the House of the Dwarf, the Casa del Adivino or Pyramid of the Magician, the tallest and steepest structure at Uxmal, whose enormous rounded pyramid still dominates the site.

The final ordeal closes the tale as a succession myth: the king must break a bundle of cogoiol wood over the dwarf's head and take a blow in return, with the ordeal held before all the grandees of the state. The old woman places a tortilla on the dwarf's head; the king shatters his whole bundle to no effect; when his own word binds him to the return blow, the dwarf strikes once and then a second time, and the king's skull breaks to pieces. The spectators proclaim the victorious dwarf their sovereign, and the old woman vanishes — only to reappear, in the tale's coda, as the water-selling woman by the subterranean river at Mani, whose serpent devours the innocent babies.

As a corpus record the episode is the Maya counterpart of the 'unfinished palace in a night' cycle (parallels exist in Irish and South American tale types) fused with a kingship-transfer myth: the dwarf's victory founds a new dynasty of the diviner's house. The Casa del Adivino's own architecture — built over and enclosing an older inner temple — was read by travelers as the material signature of the legend's claim that the dwarf's palace rose in a single night over an older world.

functions: Founding legend of the House of the Dwarf / Pyramid of the Magician at Uxmal
Succession myth: the smallest challenger replaces the proud king
Etiology of the Casa del Adivino's enclosed older inner temple

variants.name: Pyramid of the Magician in 20th-century tellings
variants.text_tradition: Twentieth-century tourist and local versions, Uxmal
variants.summary: Modern versions give the dwarf hatched from an egg by the old sorceress and named governor on the day the pyramid is finished overnight; the trials of strength are condensed to the wood bundle.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The dwarf story is still told at Uxmal and in Yucatec households; present it as living local legend, not 'mere folk tale'.

title.en: The Old Woman of Mani and the Water-Selling Serpent
title.zh: 馬尼老嫗與賣水的巨蛇

source.work: Desire Charnay, The Ancient Cities of the New World (1887), reproducing the Uxmal legend cycle of Stephens (1843)

summary.en: After the dwarf's victory the old woman disappeared; but at Mani, fifty miles away, a deep well leads to a subterraneous passage reaching as far as Merida, where an old woman sits on the bank of a river shaded by a great tree, with a serpent by her side. She sells water in small quantities and accepts no money — she must have human beings, innocent babies, which are devoured by the serpent. She is the dwarf's mother.
summary.zh: 侏儒得勝之後，老嫗消失；但在五十里外的馬尼，一口深井通向遠及梅里達的地下甬道，一老嫗坐於河畔大樹之蔭，旁有巨蛇。她零星賣水，不收金錢——她要的是人，是無辜的嬰兒，皆為巨蛇所吞。她正是侏儒之母。

sensitivity.note: Yucatec folk legend recorded by travelers; paraphrase of public-domain texts only.

passages.text: After this the old woman disappeared; but in the village of Mani, fifty miles distant, is a deep well leading to a subterraneous passage which extends as far as Merida. In this passage is an old woman sitting on the bank of a river shaded by a great tree, having a serpent by her side.
passages.note: Quoted from Charnay (1887) reproducing Stephens (1843); lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: She sells water in small quantities, accepting no money, for she must have human beings, innocent babies, which are devoured by the serpent. This old woman is the dwarf's mother — the giver of the palace gone down into the water, the price of whose gifts is still paid in children.
passages.note: Condensed from Charnay (1887) reproducing Stephens (1843); not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The House of the Old Woman

region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾

texts.period: Building named in local tradition; described by Stephens 1843

source.work: John Lloyd Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843), on the ruins of Uxmal

summary.en: Among the buildings of Uxmal, near the Governor's Palace and the House of the Turtles, stands the Casa de la Vieja — the House of the Old Woman — named in local tradition for the aged mother of the dwarf, the sorceress of the hatched egg, whose hut is remembered in the stone of the city she helped to raise.
summary.zh: 烏斯馬爾諸建築之間，在總督宮與龜屋之旁，立有名為卡薩·德拉·維赫的「老嫗之屋」——以侏儒之母、孵蛋的老巫嫗為名；傳說中其草屋所居，被記於其助建之城的石構之中。

sensitivity.note: Yucatec folk legend recorded by travelers; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: In the foreground is the inner facade of the front range of the Monjas; to the left, in the distance, appears the Casa de la Vieja, or of the Old Woman; and rising grandly above the front of the Monjas are the House of the Turtles, that of the Governor, and the Casa de Palomos, or the House of the Pigeons.
passages.note: Condensed from Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843); not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: The name preserves the old woman of the dwarf legend: the childless sorceress who hatched the egg, protected her son with a tortilla, and vanished when he became sovereign — remembered at Uxmal in a stone house, as her own hut was of thatch in the tale.
passages.note: Condensed from Stephens (1843) and the dwarf legend cycle; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Fresh Copal in the House of the Dwarf, 1656
title.zh: 1656年，侏儒之屋中仍燃新柯巴脂

region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾

texts.period: Recorded by Cogolludo 1656; reproduced in Charnay 1887

source.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), as reproduced in Charnay, The Ancient Cities of the New World (1887)

summary.en: Padre Cogolludo, who visited the temple at Uxmal in 1656, complains of the steep staircase that made his head swim, and finds in one of its apartments offerings of cocoa and copal burned very recently — fifteen years after the Conquest the natives were still sacrificing to their gods and practising their superstitions in their own temples.
summary.zh: 1656年訪烏斯馬爾神廟的科戈柳多神父，抱怨其陡階令人眩暈，並在其一室中發現不久前焚燒的可可與柯巴脂祭品——征服後十五年，土人仍在自家神廟中向其神獻祭、行其舊俗。

sensitivity.note: Colonial missionary record; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: Padre Cogolludo, who visited this temple in 1656, is the first to complain of the steep staircase, which caused his head to swim. He found in one of these apartments offerings of cocoa and copal which had been burnt very recently; consequently, fifteen years after the Conquest the natives were still sacrificing to their gods, and practising their superstitions in their own temples.
passages.note: Condensed from Charnay (1887) quoting Cogolludo; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Indians Cling to Their Ruins: The Title Papers of Uxmal
title.zh: 土人戀其遺址：烏斯馬爾地契文書

region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾

source.work: John Lloyd Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843), title papers of Uxmal

summary.en: The title papers of Uxmal record that, one hundred and forty years after the founding of Merida, the buildings were still regarded with reverence by the Indians, forming the nucleus of a scattered population resorting to them for religious rites at a distance from the eyes of the Spaniards; Cogolludo had seen in the House of the Dwarf 'the marks of copal recently burned', the evidence of some idolatry recently committed.
summary.zh: 烏斯馬爾地契文書記載：梅里達建城一百四十年後，土人仍崇敬其建築，散落的人群以之為核，避西班牙人耳目而行其祭儀；科戈柳多曾在侏儒之屋見「新焚柯巴脂之痕」，證明新近仍有偶像崇拜。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era documents; paraphrase of public-domain text only.

passages.text: The reader will perceive that we have here two distinct, independent witnesses testifying that, one hundred and forty years after the foundation of Merida, the buildings of Uxmal were regarded with reverence by the Indians; that they formed the nucleus of a dispersed and scattered population, and were resorted to for the observance of religious rites at a distance from the eyes of the Spaniards.
passages.note: Condensed from Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843); not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Cogolludo saw in the House of the Dwarf the 'marks of copal recently burned', 'the evidence of some idolatry recently committed'; and the private title papers show that it was the policy of the government to break up the Indian customs and drive the natives away from their consecrated buildings, which they were openly and notoriously worshipping in these ancient buildings.
passages.note: Condensed from Stephens (1843), on the title papers of Uxmal; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Cerro de los Sacrificios: The Mound of Sacrifice at Uxmal

region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾

texts.period: Named in local tradition; described by Charnay 1887

source.work: Desire Charnay, The Ancient Cities of the New World (1887), on Uxmal

summary.en: To the rear of the Dwarf's House rises a great pyramid crowned by a vast platform without monuments, known as the Cerro de los Sacrificios, the Mound of Sacrifice — planned like the Mexican temples, with small wooden chapels containing idols upon its summit.
summary.zh: 侏儒之屋之後，聳起一座巨大的金字塔，頂部為一空闊平台，無有任何建築，人稱塞羅·德·洛斯·薩克里菲西奧斯——祭儀之丘；其規制如墨西哥神廟，頂上原立有小木龕以奉神像。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of public-domain travel description only.

passages.text: To the rear, a great pyramid crowned by a vast platform, without monuments, known as 'Cerro de los Sacrificios', Mound of Sacrifice. It is on the plan of the Mexican temples, which consisted, like this monument, of a pyramid with small wood chapels containing idols.
passages.note: Condensed from Charnay (1887), on Uxmal; not verbatim throughout.

region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦諾卡卡布附近的希科赫

source.work: John Lloyd Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843), ruins of Xcoch

summary.en: At the ruins of Xcoch, under the high mound visible from the House of the Dwarf, Stephens explores a mysterious well: a circular cavity with a great grove, a mouth opening into passages explored by torchlight, used by the village for its water — the subterranean world beneath a Maya mound.
summary.zh: 在希科赫遺址——侏儒之屋可望見的高丘之下——斯蒂芬斯探一神秘之井：圓形井穴與秀美林地，井口通入甬道，秉炬而探；村人至今汲水於此——馬雅土丘之下別有幽冥世界。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of public-domain travel description only.

passages.text: The ruins of Xcoch: a mysterious well, with a fine grove and a circular cavity, the mouth of the well opening into passages which we explored with torches; the well was in use by the village, which drew its water from the passages under the mound — the underground world beneath a Maya ruin.
passages.note: Condensed from Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843), ch. XV; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: El Laberinto: The Mound with Secret Chambers
title.zh: 拉貝林托：藏有密室的土丘

region.en: Hacienda of San Felipe, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦聖費利佩莊園

source.work: John Lloyd Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843), the Labyrinth

summary.en: The Indians told of a subterraneous structure called El Laberinto, the Labyrinth, 'which had no end'. Entering by a half-buried door under a mound, Stephens finds long passages, branching in every direction, choked at last by fallen earth — and realizes the labyrinth runs inside the body of a great mound, giving rise to the idea that all the great mounds of the country contain secret and unknown chambers.
summary.zh: 土人言及一地下結構，名拉貝林托——迷宮，「無有盡頭」。斯蒂芬斯自丘下半掩之門而入，見甬道綿長、四向分歧，終為塌土所阻——於是恍然：迷宮竟貫穿巨大土丘之腹，由此推想，全地諸大丘之中或皆藏有未知的密室。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of public-domain travel description only.

passages.text: I was sure of going on to the end and discovering something, when all at once I found the passage choked up and effectually stopped; the ceiling had fallen in, crushed by a great mass of superincumbent earth, and farther progress was utterly impossible. I told the Indians to put an end to their lying stories about the Laberinto and its having no end.
passages.note: Condensed from Stephens, Incidents of Travel in Yucatan, vol. I (1843); not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: On examining outside, I found that what I had taken for an irregular natural formation was a pyramidal mound of the same general character with all the rest; the door of El Laberinto opened into this mound, and the labyrinth, instead of being subterraneous, was in the body of the mound — a discovery which gave rise to the exciting idea that all the great mounds scattered over the country contained secret, unknown, and hidden chambers.
passages.note: Condensed from Stephens (1843); not verbatim throughout.
